newsitem.title: UK: Researchers worry whether HRT affects mammograms.
newsitem.headline: Researchers worry whether HRT affects mammograms.

text.p: British researchers said on Friday they were worried that hormone replacement therapy (HRT) might be interfering with screening for breast cancer and urged immediate research into the matter.

Several studies have found more cases than expected of breast cancer between regular mammograms, Dr Valerie Beral of the Imperial Cancer Research Fund and colleagues wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal.
"One factor that needs to be considered is that the use of hormone replacement therapy by women screened in the UK may contribute to this relatively high rate of interval cancer," they wrote.

Earlier trials, notably one in Sweden, were done before HRT was commonly used by women complaining of menopause symptoms. HRT is prescribed to not only alleviate these symptoms but to prevent osteoporosis, or thinning of the bones.
With more and more women using HRT, they said, it was important to know whether it contributed to the measured rate of increase in breast cancers in between screenings in Britain.
Beral said HRT was known to make breast tissue more dense, and therefore made mammograms harder to read.

"HRT use is increasing and it is therefore particularly important that research is undertaken as soon as possible to see whether HRT is also resulting in more cancers being missed at screening," she said in a statement.
"We do not know whether this will turn out to be the case. There is simply not enough evidence yet to know whether more cancers are being missed among women taking HRT," she added.

"If research shows that HRT does reduce the efficacy of screening among current users and if it also shows that efficacy is restored once women stop taking it, then a simple way to reduce interval cancers may be to suggest that a woman stops using HRT for a short time, perhaps some weeks or months, before she is due to be screened."
But Beral stressed this was a "big if" and said it would take three years of research to determine if this was the case.
Women in western industrialised countries such as Britain have a one in 12 chance of developing breast cancer.

More than 180,000 cases of breast cancer are diagnosed in the United States each year, and more than 40,000 women die from it. Around 14,000 women die of breast cancer each year in Britain and Scotland has the highest rate in the world.
There is evidence that, in women over 50, mammograms can catch the tumours early enough to cut the death rate by 30 percent.
